summary:
ASTRON — Astronomical Observation Network

ASTRON is a web-based platform designed to simplify access, exploration, visualization, and analysis of astronomical observation data, with a particular focus on NASA's SPHEREx mission.

The platform aims to bridge the gap between large-scale astronomical datasets and users who want to explore them without navigating complex data archives and scientific tools manually.

Through an interactive sky map powered by Aladin Lite, users can explore celestial regions and search for available observations using sky coordinates and search radius. ASTRON connects to astronomical data services, particularly IRSA, to retrieve observation metadata and access SPHEREx data products.

Users can select and download FITS files for further exploration. Using Astropy and World Coordinate System (WCS) techniques, ASTRON provides tools to inspect FITS structures, examine spatial information, and explore spectral data at selected pixel locations.

Built with React, FastAPI, and Python's scientific computing ecosystem, ASTRON combines astronomical visualization with scientific data exploration in a unified interface.

Ultimately, ASTRON aims to make astronomical data more accessible and understandable, supporting students, researchers, and astronomy enthusiasts in exploring real scientific observations.
details:
ASTRON — Astronomical Observation Network

Project Overview

ASTRON is a web-based platform designed to make astronomical observation data more accessible, understandable, and easier to explore, with a particular focus on data from NASA's SPHEREx mission.

The platform integrates interactive sky visualization, astronomical data retrieval, and scientific data inspection into a unified workflow. Through ASTRON, users can explore regions of the sky using Aladin Lite, specify celestial coordinates and search radii, and retrieve relevant observation information from the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA). Users can also inspect SPHEREx FITS data products and explore their scientific information directly within the application.

ASTRON provides tools for examining FITS file structures, interpreting spatial information through the World Coordinate System (WCS), and retrieving spectral information at selected image-pixel coordinates.

Key Features

  • Interactive Sky Exploration: Explore celestial regions through an interactive sky map powered by Aladin Lite.
  • Astronomical Catalog Search: Search for astronomical objects and coordinates using SIMBAD.
  • SPHEREx Observation Search: Retrieve observation information and access available SPHEREx data products through IRSA's Simple Image Access (SIA2) service.
  • FITS File Inspection: Examine FITS file structures and inspect their associated scientific data.
  • Spatial Information Analysis: Interpret image coordinates and celestial positions using WCS.
  • Spectral Information Exploration: Retrieve wavelength and bandwidth information at selected image pixels using spectral WCS information.

Development and Technical Implementation

ASTRON was developed using Python and JavaScript. Its frontend is built with React, Vite, and Tailwind CSS, while its backend uses FastAPI. Astropy and NumPy support scientific data processing, and Aladin Lite provides interactive sky visualization.

The development process involved integrating external astronomical archives and catalog services while building the core data-processing capabilities required to inspect astronomical FITS products.

SIMBAD was successfully integrated as the primary astronomical catalog service. We also explored VizieR as a potential fallback catalog source to improve data availability. However, persistent request timeouts prevented us from completing and validating the VizieR integration.

During development and testing, we also encountered intermittent connection timeouts and upstream errors when querying IRSA's SIA2 service. These issues limited the consistency with which live SPHEREx observation searches could be tested. The backend implements timeout handling and upstream error responses to handle these situations explicitly.

Despite these external connectivity challenges, we continued developing and testing ASTRON's core scientific exploration features, including FITS inspection, spatial coordinate interpretation through WCS, and spectral information retrieval from available SPHEREx data products.

Challenges and Lessons Learned

Building ASTRON highlighted the challenges of developing applications that depend on distributed astronomical archives and external scientific services.

The integration process demonstrated that application reliability depends not only on the correctness of its internal implementation but also on the availability and responsiveness of external data providers.

These challenges motivated us to implement explicit error handling and provide an alternative evaluation workflow using a local SPHEREx FITS sample. This allows the core scientific data-inspection capabilities to remain accessible even when live archive services are unavailable.

Innovation and Impact

ASTRON's approach lies in connecting sky visualization, astronomical archive access, and scientific data inspection within a single application.

Rather than treating astronomical observation data as isolated files or complex archive records, ASTRON provides a workflow that connects the exploration of a sky region with the inspection of its associated scientific data.

The project emphasizes usability, accessibility, scientific relevance, and data accuracy while considering the practical challenges of handling large astronomical datasets.

Ultimately, ASTRON aims to bridge the gap between complex astronomical datasets and the people who want to explore them, encouraging greater engagement with space science and making NASA's scientific observations more approachable.

Evaluation and Testing Instructions

Important Notice: IRSA Connectivity

Due to intermittent connection timeouts and upstream errors when accessing IRSA's Simple Image Access (SIA2) service, live SPHEREx observation retrieval may not work consistently during evaluation.

To ensure that ASTRON's core scientific exploration features can still be evaluated, we provide a pre-downloaded SPHEREx FITS sample through Google Drive.

FITS Sample Download:
https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1gEY_3tZn_r4O7jW9FOb7vwV-qOQLQjkC?usp=sharing

Testing Instructions

  1. Clone or download the ASTRON repository from GitHub.
  2. Download the provided SPHEREx FITS sample using the Google Drive link above.
  3. Place the downloaded FITS file inside the astron-backend/temp/ directory.
  4. Start the ASTRON backend and frontend by following the setup instructions in the repository.
  5. Open the application and explore the FITS inspection and scientific exploration features.

Using the provided sample, evaluators can:

  • Inspect the FITS file structure and its HDUs.
  • Explore spatial information using the World Coordinate System (WCS).
  • Retrieve spectral information, including wavelength and bandwidth, at selected pixel coordinates.

Important: This alternative workflow demonstrates ASTRON's local FITS processing and scientific exploration capabilities. It does not validate live SPHEREx observation retrieval through IRSA.

GitHub Repository and Branch Information

Repository:
https://github.com/MRQyzz/astron-website

The repository contains ASTRON's source code, development history, and release documentation.

For evaluation purposes, please refer to the following branches:

  • release/astron-space-apps-demo — The prepared submission and demonstration checkpoint. This is the recommended branch for evaluating and running the submitted version of ASTRON. It includes the demo runbook and release checkpoint documentation.
  • fix/pre-demo-hardening — The development branch used for integration fixes, testing, and pre-demo improvements.
  • main — The repository's main branch.

Recommended branch for evaluation: release/astron-space-apps-demo

The release branch represents the prepared demonstration checkpoint for this submission. It should not be interpreted as a claim that all planned features or external service integrations have been fully completed.
